- If sentiment history shows strong bullish (e.g., >0.5) or bearish (e.g., < -0.5) momentum in recent days, model should adjust forecast slope to match sentiment direction, especially if forecast is flat or trending sideways.
- When true outcome shows sharp spikes (e.g., >10% from prior day), model tends to overreact and overshoot — reduce forecast slope or add early correction if sentiment is neutral or slightly bearish.
- If model forecast is consistently above true outcome (especially in early days of forecast horizon), it suggests overconfidence — apply downward bias, especially if sentiment is neutral or slightly bearish.
- If sentiment history includes recent negative sentiment (e.g., -1.0 or 0.0), model should not assume continuation of upward trend — expect mean reversion or downward correction, especially if forecast is rising.
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3-5 days of high prices followed by sharp drop), model should reduce forecast slope after peak and add early downward bias.
- If sentiment history includes recent positive sentiment but true outcome is lower than forecast, model may be overestimating momentum — reduce forecast slope or add early correction.
- If model forecast is flat or rising slowly but true outcome shows sharp upward movement, model may be underestimating momentum — increase forecast slope if sentiment is bullish.
- If sentiment history includes recent negative sentiment and true outcome is rising, model may be misinterpreting sentiment — reduce forecast slope or add early correction.
- If model forecast is consistently below true outcome (especially in early days), it suggests underconfidence — increase forecast slope if sentiment is bullish.
- If sentiment history includes recent positive sentiment and true outcome is flat or declining, model may be overestimating momentum — reduce forecast slope or add early correction.
